title: Starting a Small Business
description: Test an idea, count the costs, and set the business up properly.
wolfLine: Every pack started with one wolf and a good idea.

startup-costs.definition: What you spend to get a business going, before your first sale.
startup-costs.example: A $150 stall permit and a $220 canopy.

revenue.definition: All the money customers pay you, before any costs come out.

profit.definition: What’s left of revenue after you pay your costs.

sole-proprietorship.definition: A business owned by one person with no legal separation from them. You’re one by default when you start selling on your own.
sole-proprietorship.example: Selling bread at a market under your own name.

llc.definition: A limited liability company: a business registered with your state that keeps business debts separate from your personal money.
llc.example: Imani’s Bakery LLC, so a business lawsuit can’t take her savings.

ein.definition: Employer Identification Number: a free business tax ID from the IRS, like a Social Security number for your business.
ein.example: Needed to open some business bank accounts or hire employees.

lessons.title: From Idea to Business
lessons.summary: A business solves a problem people will pay for.

steps.title: A problem people pay to solve
steps.body: Before spending a dollar, check three things: who has this problem, will they pay to fix it, and can you deliver it for less than they’ll pay?

steps.prompt: Which is the strongest business idea?
choices: Something people already pay for, that you can do better or cheaper
A cool name with no customers yet
steps.explain: Proven demand beats a clever idea.

steps.prompt: What’s the cheapest way to test an idea?
choices: Sell a small batch to real customers
steps.explain: Real sales are the only real proof.

steps.prompt: Talking to potential customers before you build anything saves money.
steps.explain: They’ll tell you what they’d actually buy.

steps.prompt: Put these in order.
items: Spot a problem people pay to solve
steps.explain: Problem, people, proof, growth.

steps.prompt: Friends say they’d “totally buy it.” What’s better proof?
steps.explain: Compliments are free. Money isn’t.

lessons.title: Startup Costs
lessons.summary: What it takes to make the first sale.

steps.context: [[Startup costs]] are what you spend to get a business going, before your first sale.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a startup cost?
steps.explain: Spent before the first sale.

steps.prompt: Add up the startup costs.
Imani set aside $1,000 for the business. How much is left as a cushion?
Which cost will she pay again for every market?
steps.explain: The canopy and reader last. Flour doesn’t.

steps.prompt: Buying used equipment can cut startup costs a lot.
steps.explain: A secondhand canopy works the same.

steps.prompt: Should Imani use her emergency fund to start?
choices: No: use money set aside for the business
steps.explain: The emergency fund is for emergencies. A business is a choice.

lessons.title: Revenue vs. Profit
lessons.summary: Sales feel great. Profit pays you.

steps.context: [[Revenue]] is all the money customers pay you. [[Profit]] is what’s left after your costs.
steps.prompt: Which tells you whether the business is working?
steps.explain: Revenue is busy. Profit is working.

steps.prompt: You sell 60 loaves at $8 each. What’s the revenue?
Ingredients and packaging cost $3 a loaf, and the stall fee is $40. What are the total costs?
What’s the profit?
A business can have big revenue and still lose money.
steps.explain: If costs are bigger than revenue, more sales can mean bigger losses.

steps.prompt: That $260 of profit took 10 hours of baking and selling. What’s that per hour?

lessons.title: Sole Proprietor or LLC?
lessons.summary: How the law sees you and your business.

steps.context: If you start selling on your own, you’re a [[sole proprietorship]] by default: legally, you and the business are the same.
steps.prompt: What’s the risk of being a sole proprietorship?
choices: Business debts can come after your personal money
steps.explain: You and the business are the same in the eyes of the law.

steps.context: An [[LLC]] (limited liability company) is a business you register with your state. It keeps business debts separate from your personal money, for a filing fee.
steps.prompt: What’s the main reason people form an LLC?
choices: To protect personal money from business debts and lawsuits
steps.explain: A wall between the business and your savings.

steps.prompt: Sole proprietorship or LLC?
items: You’re one automatically when you start selling
You file paperwork with your state
No legal separation from your personal money
Your personal savings are shielded from business debts
Usually has a yearly state fee
The simplest way to test a small idea

steps.prompt: Forming an LLC means you pay no taxes.
steps.explain: An LLC changes your legal protection, not whether you pay tax.

steps.prompt: Testing a $500 side business, most people start as…
choices: a sole proprietor, then form an LLC as it grows
steps.explain: Start simple, protect as you grow.

steps.prompt: Who should you ask about structure as you grow?
choices: An accountant, or free advisors through the SBA and SCORE
steps.explain: Free, expert help exists.

lessons.title: Keep Business Money Separate
lessons.summary: One account for the business, one for you.

steps.prompt: Why open a separate business bank account?
choices: Clean records, easier taxes and a clear view of profit
steps.explain: Mixed money hides whether you’re making any.

steps.context: An [[EIN]] is a free business tax ID from the IRS, like a Social Security number for your business.
steps.prompt: What does an EIN cost from the IRS?
steps.explain: It’s free on IRS.gov. Sites that charge are middlemen.

steps.prompt: Mixing business and personal spending makes it hard to know if you’re profitable.
steps.explain: You can’t measure what you can’t separate.

steps.prompt: Business account or personal?
You need business money for yourself. What’s the proper way?
choices: Transfer a set amount to your personal account and record it
Use the business card at dinner
Take cash from the till and not note it
steps.explain: Clean, recorded, on purpose.

steps.prompt: Setting up business money. Put it in order.
items: Get an EIN if you need one
Run all sales and costs through it
steps.explain: ID, account, discipline, paycheck.

lessons.title: Test Before You Quit
lessons.summary: Find out if people buy, as cheaply as possible.

steps.prompt: Which risks less money to learn whether people will buy?
steps.explain: A $719 experiment vs. a $36,600 one.

steps.prompt: Plan B: 50 markets at $40, plus $719 of setup. Cost for the year?
When does a shop start to make sense?
choices: When the stall keeps selling out and you know your numbers
steps.explain: Let demand pull you into bigger costs.

steps.prompt: Keeping your job while testing a business lowers the risk a lot.
steps.explain: Your rent is covered while you learn.

steps.prompt: What’s the safest way to fund a small start?
choices: Savings set aside for the business
steps.explain: Money you can afford to risk.

steps.prompt: A friend offers $5,000 for “part of the business.” What do you need?
choices: A written agreement on what they own and get back
steps.explain: Friendships survive clear paperwork better than vague promises.

steps.prompt: A $10,000 loan at 12% a year. Interest in the first year if you don’t repay any of it?
Many small businesses start with very little money and grow from their own profits.
steps.explain: Slow and self-funded is a real path.

steps.prompt: Business grants are…
choices: money you don’t repay, but competitive and with rules
steps.explain: Worth applying for, not worth counting on.

steps.prompt: Before borrowing for a business, you should know…
choices: how the business will make the payments
steps.explain: Debt needs a plan to pay it back.

lessons.title: Imani’s Bakery Stall
lessons.summary: One month of a real small business, by the numbers.

story.title: Saturday bread
story.body:
Imani works weekdays at a dental office and sells bread at a Saturday market. In her first month she went to **4** markets.

She sold **210** loaves at **$8** each. Ingredients and packaging cost **$3** a loaf, and the stall costs **$40** per market. Baking and selling took her **36** hours.

steps.prompt: What was her revenue for the month?
What did ingredients and packaging cost?
What did the stall fees cost?
What was her profit?
What’s her profit per hour? Round to the cent.
What should Imani do with the profit first?
steps.explain: Business profit is taxable income.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Starting a Business
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Revenue $900, costs $540. What’s the profit?
What’s the main reason to form an LLC?
choices: Protect personal money from business debts
steps.explain: Liability protection.

steps.prompt: An EIN from the IRS is free.
steps.explain: Don’t pay a website for it.

steps.prompt: What’s the cheapest way to test a business idea?
choices: Sell a small batch to real customers
steps.explain: Proof before spending.
